A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same dual-band thermal separation work, with matching authors, methods and experiments despite the revised title. All pages, equations, figures, tables and Appendices A-B are readable and support comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original thermal simulations, material-emissivity calibration measurements, real-scene separation results and contact-temperature validation in Figures 3-5, with additional analyses in Appendix B.

after.justification: v2 retains original simulation and real-scene measurements and adds baseline comparisons, emissivity-sensitivity results and spatial error analyses in Figures 2-3 and 6 and Tables 1-2.

M1.justification: The calibrated temperature solution, temporal emissivity-ratio constraints, optimized noise and smooth signals, and five weighted loss terms remain equivalent. Algorithm 1 documents the existing optimization procedure; its newly disclosed initialization and stopping descriptions do not establish a changed method.

E1.justification: The material-specific simulations replace asphalt with sandstone while retaining steel, quartz and black paint (v1 Figure 3; v2 Figure 10). The real-object materials and separation scenarios remain the same; the relocated fingerprint/reflection demonstration is not new coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds Blackbody Channel Prior as an evaluated comparator in both simulations and real-scene separation, and adds FLIR's reflector method to emissivity-calibration comparisons. These substantially broaden comparison beyond v1's dual-wavelength pyrometry and naive least-squares baselines, which are retained.

E3.justification: v2 adds emissivity-error evaluation at 28, 34 and 40 dB, frame-averaged spatial temperature errors in degrees Celsius, and SNR-averaged ablation reductions. Existing real-data hardware and spectral bands remain unchanged. Figure 10 mentions least-squares run selection against ground truth, whereas the main text retains minimum-objective selection; an actual change to that protocol is unresolved.

E4.justification: v2 adds targeted sensitivity analysis across true emissivity and noise levels, plus spatial error maps locating reconstruction errors (Figures 2-3). The loss-removal and filter-conditioning analyses already appear in v1 Appendix B and remain in v2; Table 1 summarizes the existing loss-ablation study rather than introducing a new ablation.

E5.justification: Both versions report five random initializations for naive least squares. Neither adds seed values, confidence intervals, significance tests or uncertainty estimates across repeated experiments. The additional averages and error curves do not introduce statistical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial comparison and diagnostic results, including BCP temperature errors of 14.6% for wineglass and 6.62% for coffee pot, reflector-method emissivities in Table 2, and emissivity-sensitivity and spatial-error results. Table 1 newly quantifies loss-term contributions. The retained uncalibrated method's corresponding real-scene errors remain 1.72% and 5.34%; the additions do not establish improved performance of that method.

T1.justification: The image-formation equations, rank-two factorization, temporal-ratio derivations and closed-form solutions remain mathematically equivalent. v2 explains the wavelength-independent background already implicit in v1's shared background-temperature variable. Consolidating derivative equations and correcting notation do not add a substantive derivation or proof.

C1.justification: The central contribution remains calibrated and uncalibrated dual-band separation of dynamic emission and reflection. v2's introduction adds the specific claim that its calibration matches the reflector method for high-emissivity materials and improves on it for low-emissivity materials, extending the claimed comparative validation.

C2.justification: v2 adds a background-averaging rationale, attributes boundary errors to reduced thermal contrast, and explains the reflector comparison through specular-reflection calibration. The original background-correlation and sensor-sensitivity limitations remain. Its new main-text description of choosing the highest condition number conflicts with the retained appendix explanation specifying the lowest.

D1.justification: Algorithm 1 newly specifies zero/random initializations and a loss-change stopping condition, and the title page adds a project-page address. Hardware, filter specifications and Appendix A calibration instructions are retained. The supplied PDFs do not establish that downloadable code or data became available.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially expands positioning against point thermometry, reflection suppression, contrast enhancement and thermal polarization methods. BCP, already cited in v1, receives a specific discussion of its assumptions and differences from this work. Added literature includes Krapez on thermometry ambiguity and recent thermal-polarization studies, accompanied by more detailed distinctions from prior approaches.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, related work and substantial portions of the optimization narrative are rewritten. Method subsections are consolidated, experiments are organized into simulation and real-data subsections, and limitations become a separate section. This is extensive editorial restructuring beyond the addition of scientific content.

P2.justification: v2 relocates the opening demonstration to Figure 5 and the revised material-specific plots to Appendix Figure 10. It adds summary and spatial-error displays, two tables and an algorithm block, reorders the calibration figure, and redesigns the real-results grid with a BCP column and reordered methods. These substantially change visual presentation.

improvement.justification: Compared with v1, the BCP and reflector comparisons strengthen empirical validation, while emissivity-sensitivity and spatial-error analyses make performance boundaries easier to assess. The reorganized narrative and procedural disclosure also help. These gains are moderated by conflicting filter-conditioning and least-squares run-selection descriptions, leaving a useful but limited overall improvement.
